"So are you going to apply to the science camp?" Jahnavi asked, putting the form on the table.
"Maybe." Akash raised one eyebrow at the paper.
"That's your third maybe this week."
"I know." He picked at the corner of the form. "The others have done coding for years. I'll be the one who doesn't know anything."
"Is it that you don't want to go, or that you're scared it'll go badly?"
He thought about it. "Scared, I think. But also I'm not sure it's even the right camp."
"Both of those are worth looking at. I won't push. Shall we read the syllabus together tonight and list what worries you?"
"Okay." He almost smiled. "Maybe that helps."

qa.q: What does Jahnavi say about Akash's maybe this week?
qa.a: Jahnavi says it's Akash's third maybe this week.

qa.q: What might Akash be feeling about the science camp?
qa.a: He is probably nervous about not knowing enough compared with the others, and also unsure about whether it suits him, so his doubt mixes fear and careful thinking.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi and Akash do next?
qa.a: They could read the syllabus together and list his worries, sorting the fears from the real questions before he decides.

qa.q: Why might Jahnavi's choice not to push matter to Akash?
qa.a: Pressure could make him feel he had to say yes to please Jahnavi, while open discussion lets him work out what he really thinks. 🙂

grounding: A teen hesitates and says maybe about a plan, and open discussion works better than pressure.

passage: When Keerthana asked if I'd join the robotics team with her, I said "maybe" and raised one eyebrow, the way I do. She took it as a no. I took it as honest. Truthfully I was arguing with myself: part of me loved the idea, part of me was scared of being the only one who had never soldered anything, and part of me wondered if I was just copying her. She could have called me a coward. Instead she asked, "Which part are you unsure about?" That made me look properly. I said the scared part. Then the doubt started to shrink, because now it had a name and we could talk about it. I joined in the end, but I asked questions first. - Ayesha

qa.q: What did Ayesha say when Keerthana suggested joining the robotics team?
qa.a: Ayesha said 'maybe' and raised one eyebrow.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when saying maybe?
qa.a: Ayesha was torn, with love for the idea, fear of being the only one who had never soldered anything, and a worry about just copying Keerthana.

qa.q: What did Keerthana do that made the doubt easier to handle?
qa.a: She asked which part Ayesha was unsure about, so the doubt could be named and discussed instead of pushed away.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have first read Ayesha's 'maybe'?
qa.a: She took it as a no, which shows that a hesitation can be read in more than one way.

grounding: A teen's maybe and raised brow reflect a mix of fear and careful thinking, and open discussion beats pressure.

passage:
Class 9 note - Siddharth (class teacher), Tuesday
When the class voted to hold our charity bake sale at the mall on Saturday, almost every hand went up. Bhavna's went halfway, then down. She raised an eyebrow and said, "Maybe... I'm not sure."
A few students groaned. Someone said, "Don't spoil it."
I asked the class to let her speak. She said, slowly, "Doesn't the mall need permission? And who's bringing the oven? And if it rains, how do we get the cakes there?"
Three good questions. Nobody had thought of any of them.
Her doubt came from careful thinking, not from being negative. I told the class so. We made a list of what we'd need to check.
Bhavna volunteered to phone the mall office. On Thursday she told us they needed a letter from the school, and it took two days, so we moved the sale to the following week.

qa.q: How many questions did Bhavna ask?
qa.a: Three good questions.

qa.q: What might Bhavna have been feeling when her hand went halfway up?
qa.a: Bhavna seemed unsure and hesitant, holding real doubts about the plan, and possibly a little nervous about going against the class.

qa.q: What did Siddharth do that helped?
qa.a: He asked the class to let Bhavna speak, took her doubts seriously as careful thinking, and turned them into a checklist.

qa.q: How might the students who groaned have seen Bhavna's doubt at first?
qa.a: They probably saw it as spoiling the fun, not realising she was spotting real problems with the plan.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a teenager's hesitation and "maybe" reflecting careful thinking, and open discussion working better than pressure.

passage:
Monday
Maria wants us both to try out for the district basketball team on Saturday. She's so excited. I said, "Maybe," and changed the subject.
Truth: I'm scared. Not of the game. Of the trial. Of standing in front of coaches I don't know and missing every shot. Of Maria getting in and me not.
Maria noticed. She said, "You don't have to. But can I ask what the 'maybe' is about?"
I told her. All of it.
She didn't say "you'll be fine." She said, "I'm scared too. Of the new coaches. Want to go together, and if either of us doesn't get in, we still get pizza?"
That made it smaller.
I think I'm going. Still scared. But the maybe is more of a yes now.
- Nazia

qa.q: When are the district basketball trials?
qa.a: On Saturday.

qa.q: What feeling was behind Nazia's "maybe"?
qa.a: Nazia was afraid of the trial, of missing shots in front of unfamiliar coaches, and of Maria getting in while Nazia didn't.

qa.q: Why did Maria's response work better than pressure?
qa.a: She asked what the doubt was about, shared her own fear, and offered a plan that made it safer, instead of pushing.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt when Nazia said maybe?
qa.a: Maria may have felt a bit disappointed at first, but cared enough to ask rather than push.

grounding: The diary shows a teenager's doubt coming from fear, and a friend's open question working better than pressure.

passage: Chaitanya had the whole plan sketched on the back of a bus ticket: cycle the twenty kilometres to the waterfall on Sunday, swim, back by dark. "You're coming, right?" he asked Joseph outside the village shop. Joseph turned the ticket over, one eyebrow up. "Maybe." "Maybe? You're scared." Joseph shrugged, and Chaitanya nearly pushed harder, then noticed Joseph didn't look scared so much as thoughtful; he was frowning at the sky over the hills, where clouds were already stacking up. "Okay," Chaitanya said. "What's the maybe about?" "The radio said heavy rain from Saturday. Last monsoon the stream near the fall rose in an hour. And my back brake is half gone." He paused. "And yes, a bit scared. Both." Chaitanya chewed on that. "So... next Sunday, if it's dry, and we fix your brake first at Salim's shop?" Joseph's eyebrow came down. "Now that's a yes."

qa.q: How far is the waterfall?
qa.a: The waterfall is twenty kilometres away.

qa.q: What feelings were behind Joseph's 'Maybe'?
qa.a: Joseph's doubt was mostly careful thinking about heavy rain, the rising stream and a weak brake, mixed with some honest fear, as the word 'Both' admits.

qa.q: What turned the 'maybe' into a yes?
qa.a: Chaitanya stopped pushing, asked what the maybe was about, and changed the plan to a dry Sunday with the brake fixed first. 👍

qa.q: How did Chaitanya first read the raised eyebrow?
qa.a: Chaitanya first took it as fear and nearly pushed harder, before noticing Joseph was watching the clouds.

grounding: It shows a teenager's hesitation and 'maybe' reflecting both careful thinking and fear, and open discussion working better than pressure.
